s3.quote: Elders, the gods have righted one again
s3.note: Creon's first word is plain ἄνδρες (_andres_, 'men', l. 162), and his first subject is θεοὶ (_theoi_, 'the gods'), placed at the end of the line for weight. He opens by crediting heaven with the victory. Hold on to that, because this scene ends with him telling the same old men that it is 'intolerable' to suggest the gods had anything to do with the burial. He is pious as long as the gods agree with the government.

s3.quote: Our storm-tossed ship of state, now safe in port.
s3.note: Storr has built the ship and the harbour himself. The Greek (l. 163) says only that the gods, having shaken the city's affairs πολλῷ σάλῳ (_pollōi salōi_, 'in a great sea-swell'), ὤρθωσαν (_ōrthōsan_, 'set them upright') again. The same gods do the shaking and the righting. The word to track is the 'upright' one: Oedipus 'kept the city upright' at l. 167, the city sails 'upright' at l. 190, and in [[s11]] Teiresias will remind Creon that he once steered this city straight, just before telling him he has run it aground.

s3.quote: But you by special summons I convened
s3.note: The Greek is ἐκ πάντων δίχα (_ek pantōn dicha_, 'apart from everyone', l. 164). This is a hand-picked audience, old men chosen for a record of obedience, and the people are not asked. Haemon will tell his father in [[s7]] what the unpicked city is saying. Ask who is on stage: a king one day in office, fifteen elders, attendants, and nobody who can say no.

s3.quote: I knew you loyal to Laius of old;
s3.note: Loyal is too mild. He says they were σέβοντας (_sebontas_, 'revering', l. 166) the power of Laius' throne, and _sebein_ is the verb of religious awe. From his second sentence Creon uses the vocabulary of worship for obedience to rulers. The play's quarrel over _eusebeia_, what reverence is and to whom it is owed, begins here, before Antigone has been mentioned.

s3.quote: Brother by brother murderously slain,
s3.note: Storr's 'murderously' covers a harder phrase: αὐτόχειρι σὺν μιάσματι (_autocheiri syn miasmati_, 'with the pollution of a kindred hand', l. 172). Creon knows what _miasma_ is and names it in his first minute. He will then manufacture a larger one by leaving a corpse above ground, and it is the pollution, carried by birds to the altars, that Teiresias reports in [[s11]]. Note also _autocheir_, 'own-handed': it comes back at l. 306 in a place Creon does not intend.

s3.quote: By right of kinship to the Princes dead,
s3.note: ἀγχιστεῖα (_anchisteia_, l. 174) is a legal word, 'nearness of kin', the title under which an Athenian inherited. The same nearness carried the duty to bury the dead man. Creon claims the throne by his kinship with the brothers and in the next breath forbids the chief office kinship imposes. Antigone never makes this point against him, but the audience had the law in their heads.

s3.quote: I claim and hold the throne and sovereignty.
s3.note: The line begins ἐγὼ (_egō_, l. 173) and has πάντα, 'all', in the middle: 'I hold all the powers and the throne.' Count the first-person pronouns in this speech; they come at ll. 164, 173, 178, 184, 191, and twice in the last four lines. A man who has just said power is the test of character has started the test.

s3.quote: The temper of a man, his mind and will,
s3.note: Three nouns: ψυχήν τε καὶ φρόνημα καὶ γνώμην (_psychēn te kai phronēma kai gnōmēn_, l. 176), soul, cast of mind, judgment. The middle one, _phronēma_, is Creon's word. He closes this speech with it at l. 207, and the Chorus hand it back in the ode at l. 354. It belongs to the family of _phronein_, 'to think soundly', which is the last thing the play says anyone learns.

s3.quote: Till he be proved by exercise of power;
s3.note: The Greek is physical: until a man is shown ἐντριβὴς (_entribēs_, 'rubbed, worn', l. 177) against ἀρχαῖς τε καὶ νόμοισιν, 'offices and laws'. Storr keeps the offices and drops the laws. The thought was proverbial, and Greeks credited one of the Seven Sages with the saying that rule shows the man. Creon sets the terms of his own examination, and the rest of the play is the test he asks for here, failed by his own standard.

s3.quote: Swerve from the highest policy, tongue-tied
s3.note: The bad ruler is one who keeps γλῶσσαν ἐγκλῄσας (_glōssan enklēisas_, 'his tongue locked up', l. 180) ἐκ φόβου, out of fear. That is a fair maxim for a king and an exact description of his subjects by the end of the day. Antigone tells him in [[s5]] that the elders would approve her if fear did not shut their mouths, and the guards in this very scene bow their heads φόβῳ (l. 270). He also praises 'the best counsels' here and will refuse every piece of counsel offered him until Teiresias has left.

s3.quote: And I contemn the man who sets his friend
s3.note: φίλον (_philon_, l. 183) is the word, and 'friend' is too thin for it. A _philos_ is first of all one's own: kin, household, those to whom one is bound before any choosing. Antigone used it of Polyneices in [[s1]]. Creon says that whoever counts a _philos_ above his fatherland he counts 'nowhere', οὐδαμοῦ λέγω. He is ranking family beneath the city in general terms, before he knows the offender will be his niece and his son's bride.

s3.quote: To witness Zeus, whose eyes are everywhere,
s3.note: ἴστω Ζεὺς (_istō Zeus_, 'let Zeus know it', l. 184): the first of two oaths by Zeus in this episode; the second is at l. 304. A Zeus who sees everything always also sees the body on the plain. In [[s5]] Antigone's opening move is that it was not Zeus who made this proclamation. Both of them call the same witness.

s3.quote: If I perceive some mischievous design
s3.note: Storr turns a great word into a conspiracy. Creon says he would not be silent on seeing τὴν ἄτην (_tēn atēn_, 'ruin, the blindness that leads to ruin', l. 185) 'walking toward the citizens in place of safety'. _Atē_ is the subject of [[s6|the second stasimon]], where it is the thing that walks through a house generation after generation. Here it is on its way to the townsmen and the man watching for it is the one bringing it. The pairing of _atē_ with safety returns in the last line of his next speech (l. 314).

s3.quote: Nor would I reckon as my private friend
s3.note: 'Private' and 'public' are Storr's antithesis. The Greek is blunter: 'I would never make a man hostile to the land a _philos_ for myself' (ll. 187–188), with δυσμενῆ, 'ill-minded', standing against φίλον. The verb is the telling part. For Creon a _philos_ is something you appoint. Polyneices is his sister's son and was his _philos_ before either of them could choose.

s3.quote: Is the good ship that holds our fortunes all:
s3.note: ἡ σῴζουσα (_hē sōizousa_, 'she who keeps us safe', l. 189): the city is the saviour, and the ship appears only in the next word, πλέοντες, 'sailing'. This is where the image Storr planted in the first line actually stands in the Greek. It is an old and honourable figure, and Creon is not wrong that everyone drowns when the ship goes down. What he leaves out is that the helmsman can sink her. In [[s13]] he calls what he has reached a harbour of Hades.

s3.quote: Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck.
s3.note: Storr gives a sigh where the Greek gives a doctrine. Literally: 'only while we sail on her upright do we make our friends', τοὺς φίλους ποιούμεθα (_tous philous poioumetha_, l. 190). Friends are made, on the deck of the city, and by implication unmade there. This is _philos_ redefined by the polis: for Antigone you are born with your _philoi_ and cannot resign from them. The whole collision of [[s5]] is contained in that one verb.

s3.quote: Such is the policy by which I seek
s3.note: 'Policy' is νόμοισι (_nomoisi_, 'laws, principles', l. 191): 'by such _nomoi_ I make this city great.' It is Creon's first use of _nomos_ for his own maxims. The Chorus will say at l. 213 that he may use any _nomos_ he pleases, and Antigone will answer in [[s5]] with laws nobody enacted. Watch how easily a ruler's rules of thumb become 'the laws' when he is the one speaking.

s3.quote: I have proclaimed an edict as concerns
s3.note: Storr's 'conformably' in the line above stands for ἀδελφὰ τῶνδε (_adelpha tōnde_, 'brother to these', l. 192): the decree is 'brother' to his principles. The metaphor is ordinary Greek for 'akin', but it is a strange word to reach for when introducing an order about two brothers. The verb is κηρύξας, 'having had it heralded'. Antigone will insist on that word: a herald's proclamation, a _kērygma_, which she will not allow to be a law.

s3.quote: That are the guerdon of the heroic dead.
s3.note: The Greek says the rites 'go down to the best of the dead below', τοῖς ἀρίστοις ... κάτω νεκροῖς (l. 197). Creon believes that what is done at a grave reaches someone underneath. He is no rationalist about burial; he knows what the offerings are for and is deliberately withholding them. That makes the next clause an act against the dead man and the powers below, and it is how Teiresias will describe it.

s3.quote: But for the miscreant exile who returned
s3.note: 'Miscreant' is Storr's word. What Creon says first is τὸν δʼ αὖ ξύναιμον τοῦδε, 'but his brother of the same blood', and ξύναιμον (_xynaimon_, l. 198) is one of the play's kinship words. He states the tie in his own decree and then legislates as if it were not there. φυγὰς (l. 200), 'an exile', is the only hint of Polyneices' side of the story, and nobody on stage takes it up.

s3.quote: His father’s city and his father’s gods,
s3.note: θεοὺς τοὺς ἐγγενεῖς (_theous tous engeneis_, 'the gods of his race', l. 199). The charge is sacrilege as well as treason, and Creon repeats it with more heat at ll. 285–287. It matters to his reasoning: he infers that the gods must hate the man who came to burn their temples. That is an inference about the gods' feelings, and at no point does he ask a god or a prophet.

s3.quote: And glut his vengeance with his kinsmen’s blood,
s3.note: αἵματος κοινοῦ πάσασθαι (_haimatos koinou pasasthai_, 'to taste of shared blood', ll. 201–202): Creon makes him a cannibal. The adjective κοινοῦ, 'common, shared', is the one Antigone opens the play with, in her first line, addressed to her sister's head. For her the shared blood is the bond that obliges; for Creon it is the aggravation of the crime. They use the same word and mean opposite things by it.

s3.quote: For Polyneices ’tis ordained that none
s3.note: After a speech full of 'I', the decree itself comes in the impersonal perfect passive: ἐκκεκήρυκται (_ekkekēryktai_, 'it stands proclaimed', l. 203), 'to this city'. The author disappears at the moment of the order and the polis is put in his place. When Haemon asks in [[s7]] whether the city belongs to one man, this grammatical sleight is what he is exposing.

s3.quote: Shall give him burial or make mourn for him,
s3.note: Two prohibitions, μήτε κτερίζειν μήτε κωκῦσαί (l. 204): no funeral gifts and no keening. _Kōkyein_ is the shrill wail of women at a death, and the Guard will use a compound of it when he describes Antigone over the body in [[s5]]. Laying out and lamenting were women's work in a Greek household, so the edict, though addressed to 'anyone', falls on the two surviving women of the family. For the Athenian audience: a traitor could be refused burial in Attic soil, but his kin might bury him across the border. Creon forbids burial anywhere and posts a watch.

s3.quote: For dogs and carrion crows, a ghastly sight.
s3.note: The last word in the Greek is ἰδεῖν (_idein_, 'to look upon', l. 206): the body is to be eaten and αἰκισθέν, 'disfigured', for people to see. He is making an exhibit as well as withholding honour. The birds are οἰωνῶν (_oiōnōn_, l. 205), the word for birds of omen too, and it is exactly these birds, gorged on this flesh, whose cries Teiresias can no longer read in [[s11]]. The audience would also hear the opening of the _Iliad_, where dogs and birds get the bodies of heroes.

s3.quote: So am I purposed; never by my will
s3.note: τοιόνδʼ ἐμὸν φρόνημα, 'such is my _phronēma_' (l. 207), the word from l. 176. He said a man's _phronēma_ cannot be known until he rules, and thirty lines later he displays his, complete. The speech that began with the gods righting the city ends twice with 'from me': ἔκ γʼ ἐμοῦ here and ἐξ ἐμοῦ at l. 210. Honour in Thebes now has a single source.

s3.quote: But all good patriots, alive or dead,
s3.note: θανὼν καὶ ζῶν ὁμοίως (_thanōn kai zōn homoiōs_, 'dead and living alike', ll. 209–210). Here is the overreach, stated as a boast: his jurisdiction covers the dead on the same terms as the living. The one test is being εὔνους, 'well-minded', toward the city. The Chorus pick the phrase up at l. 214 and hand it back to him with the order reversed.

s3.quote: Son of Menoeceus, thus thou will’st to deal
s3.note: ἀρέσκει (_areskei_, 'it pleases', l. 211): 'this is your pleasure, Creon'. The elders report his wish and add no word of their own. Compare what a compliant chorus could have said: wisely spoken, justly decreed. They address him by his father's name rather than as king, which may be courtesy and may be a reminder that he is new.

s3.quote: Thy word is law; thou canst dispose of us
s3.note: Read this coldly. νόμῳ δὲ χρῆσθαι παντί (_nomōi de chrēsthai panti_, l. 213): 'you have the power, I suppose, to use any law at all, about the dead and about us who live.' The little particle που, 'I suppose', is in the Greek and not in Storr. They describe his power and decline to praise his judgment. When Antigone claims in [[s5]] that the city agrees with her and is afraid to say so, this line is her evidence.

s3.quote: See then ye execute what I ordain.
s3.note: He asks them to be σκοποὶ (_skopoi_, 'watchers', l. 215) of his orders. They take it, or choose to take it, as a request to guard the corpse, and plead their age. He means something else: watch the city for me. Two lines later he has ἐπίσκοποι, 'overseers', on the body already. A regime one day old has sentries on a dead man and wants informers among the elders.

s3.quote: On younger shoulders lay this grievous charge.
s3.note: This is the first refusal in the play after Ismene's, and it is made by old men with perfect manners. They do not say the task is wrong. They say it is heavy and they are old. It is the Chorus's method throughout: never oppose, never quite endorse, until Teiresias gives them cover in [[s11]].

s3.quote: Not to connive at disobedience.
s3.note: τοῖς ἀπιστοῦσιν (_tois apistousin_, 'those who disobey', l. 219): he already assumes there will be some. The verb also means 'to disbelieve, to withhold trust', which suits a ruler who equates the two. The Chorus use the same participle of Antigone when she is led in at l. 381, so his category is ready for her before she fills it.

s3.quote: No man is mad enough to court his death.
s3.note: μῶρος (_mōros_, 'fool', l. 220), and the verb is ἐρᾷ (_erai_, 'is in love with'): no one is such a fool as to be in love with dying. We have just watched a scene in which someone was. In [[s1]] Antigone said it would be fine to die doing this, and Ismene told her she was in love with the impossible, using the same verb. The elders state as a law of human nature the exact thing the audience knows to be false. Antigone will throw 'fool' back at Creon in [[s5]].

s3.quote: The penalty _is_ death: yet hope of gain
s3.note: The first appearance of τὸ κέρδος (_to kerdos_, 'gain, profit', l. 222), and note where it comes: before any crime has been reported. Creon has the motive ready in advance. Death he calls ὁ μισθός, 'the wage', so even the penalty is put in terms of pay. From here to the end of the scene he explains everything by money, and in [[s11]] he will say the same of Teiresias. Antigone will use _kerdos_ once, in [[s5]], for dying before her time, which is the one gain he has not budgeted for.

s3.quote: My lord, I will not make pretense to pant
s3.note: Messengers in tragedy arrive at a run with their news already in their mouths. This one opens by announcing that he has not hurried, a joke at the convention's expense. He is nameless, a common soldier, and the only comic figure in the play. He speaks the same iambic trimeter as the king, but the syntax is that of talk: restarts, proverbs, reported arguments with himself. Sophocles lowers the register exactly when the plot's first shock is due.

s3.quote: In sooth my soul beneath its pack of thought
s3.note: The pack, and conscience with her spur and curb two lines on, are Storr's. The Greek has φροντίδων ἐπιστάσεις (_phrontidōn epistaseis_, 'haltings of thought', l. 225) and then ψυχὴ γὰρ ηὔδα, 'for my soul kept saying to me' (l. 227). There is no conscience in it; the argument is about which course will hurt less. It is a small parody of tragic deliberation, and worth noticing that he is the only character who weighs both sides aloud before acting. The heroes of this play do not deliberate.

s3.quote: Thus leisurely I hastened on my road;
s3.note: A lovely contradiction in Storr, and a textual question underneath it. This Greek text reads ἤνυτον σχολῇ βραδύς (_ēnyton scholēi bradys_, l. 231), 'I got it done, at leisure, slowly'. Storr's paradox translates a variant, _tachys_, 'quick', which many editors have preferred because it is funnier. Either way the dithering is the play's picture of ordinary fear under this king, and it is the natural product of the speech we have just heard.

s3.quote: Much thought extends a furlong to a league.
s3.note: The Greek is a flat proverb, ὁδὸς βραχεῖα γίγνεται μακρά (_hodos bracheia gignetai makra_, l. 232): 'a short road becomes long'. The Guard thinks in ready-made sayings, and there is another at l. 277. Storr's furlong and league dress him up. The line also tells us, in passing, that the corpse lies a short way from the palace.

s3.quote: To face thee. I will speak though I say nothing.
s3.note: τὸ μηδὲν (_to mēden_, 'the nothing', l. 234): his report has a hole where the culprit should be. He has an event and no agent, which is the worst thing to bring to a ruler who needs someone to blame. The phrase comes back at the end of the play, when Creon calls himself a man who is no more than nothing.

s3.quote: For plucking courage from despair methought,
s3.note: Storr reverses the Greek, which says he comes δεδραγμένος (_dedragmenos_, 'clutching tight', l. 235) to hope, τῆς ἐλπίδος: the hope that nothing can happen to him except τὸ μόρσιμον, what is fated. Fatalism is his comfort. Hope runs through these two sections: it destroys men in Creon's mouth at l. 221, the Guard clings to it here and is saved 'beyond hope' at l. 330, and the ode gives man skill 'beyond hope' at l. 365.

s3.quote: I neither did the deed nor saw it done,
s3.note: He asks to state τἀμαυτοῦ, 'my own position', first, and does so before any news. After forty lines of Creon on putting the city before oneself, the first citizen we meet puts himself before everything and says so. His phrase for the culprit is ὁ δρῶν (_ho drōn_, 'the doer', l. 239), a masculine participle. Everyone in this scene assumes a man.

s3.quote: The bearer of dread tidings needs must quake.
s3.note: Here is the word of the coming ode, ninety lines early: τὰ δεινὰ (_ta deina_, 'terrible things', l. 243) 'lay on a man much hesitation'. The Guard means frightening news. When the Chorus open [[s4]] with πολλὰ τὰ δεινά they repeat his phrase, and he will plant the adjective once more at l. 323a. The audience hear 'wondrous' in the ode with 'dreadful' already in their ears.

s3.quote: Well, it must out; the corpse is buried; someone
s3.note: After twenty-odd lines of preface the news takes three. The Greek order is the corpse, then τις, 'someone', then the participle θάψας, 'having buried', and at once βέβηκε, 'is gone' (ll. 245–246). 'Buried' is the Guard's own word for a sprinkling of dust. Ritually he is right: the handful of earth and the due rites make a burial, whatever the depth.

s3.quote: E’en now besprinkled it with thirsty dust,
s3.note: διψίαν κόνιν (_dipsian konin_, ll. 246–247), 'thirsty dust', and Storr is exact. Dry dust on a dry plain at the end of the summer's fighting, and thirsty also for the libations Antigone brings in [[s5]]. This is the image the episode is named for: a king has spoken for fifty lines, and the answer is a handful of dust.

s3.quote: Performed the proper ritual—and was gone.
s3.note: κἀφαγιστεύσας ἃ χρή (_kaphagisteusas ha chrē_, 'and having performed the rites that are due', l. 247). The soldier reporting a capital crime describes it as doing what one ought, χρή, without noticing. Creon used a cousin of the verb, ἀφαγνίσαι, at l. 196 for the rites Eteocles is to receive. So the offence is that Polyneices has been given what Creon himself calls the proper thing.

s3.quote: What say’st thou? Who hath dared to do this thing?
s3.note: Storr's 'who' drops a word: τίς ἀνδρῶν (_tis andrōn_, 'what man', l. 248). Creon asks which of the men did it, and the possibility of a woman does not occur to him here or anywhere before she is brought in. His word for the act is ὁ τολμήσας, 'the one who dared', and _tolma_, daring, is what the ode condemns in its last stanza. Half of his fury in [[s5]] comes from having asked this question in this form.

s3.quote: Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground,
s3.note: The Guard proves the burial by listing what was absent: no pick, no mattock, no wheel-rut, the ground στύφλος, hard, and unbroken. Put this beside the first stanza of [[s4]], where man's mark on the earth is the plough that wears her down year after year. Whoever buried Polyneices left the earth as it was. The act that defies the city is, by the ode's own measure, the least violent thing a human does in the play.

s3.quote: No sign that human hands had been at work.
s3.note: Storr goes a step past the Greek, which says the doer was ἄσημος (_asēmos_, 'one who left no mark', l. 252). That is the first of the play's cruxes. Why are there two burials, this one and the one Antigone is caught at in [[s5]]? Some readers have held that the gods performed the first, and the Chorus say so at once. Others say that Antigone did both and came back because the guards swept the body bare. I think Sophocles wants both thoughts available: she did it, and it looked like something a god might do.

s3.quote: When the first sentry of the morning watch
s3.note: ἡμεροσκόπος (_hēmeroskopos_, 'day-watcher', l. 253) fixes the time. The prologue was played before dawn and Antigone left it at l. 99, so she did this in the dark while the Chorus were singing in the sunrise. Storr's 'terror-stricken' in the next line translates θαῦμα δυσχερὲς (_thauma duscheres_, l. 254), 'an uncomfortable wonder'. The guards' first reaction is astonishment, which is the right preparation for an ode about wonders.

s3.quote: The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth,
s3.note: ἠφάνιστο (_ēphanisto_, 'had been made unseen', l. 255). Set that against the end of the edict, where the body was to be left for people 'to look upon'. Creon wanted a sight and the dust removes exactly that. The burial is ritually slight and answers precisely the purpose of the order.

s3.quote: To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead:
s3.note: ἄγος (_agos_, 'pollution, guilt before the gods', l. 256): the dust lay 'as of one avoiding _agos_'. The Guard takes it for the minimum any passer-by owes a corpse so as not to be tainted by having left it. So even the soldiers read the act as a religious one, and their reading condemns the order they are enforcing. Creon knows the idea: in [[s7]] he leaves Antigone a little food in her tomb to keep _agos_ off the city, using this word.

s3.quote: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign.
s3.note: The jackal is Storr's; the Greek says 'beast or dog'. This is the detail that makes it uncanny, since a film of dust would keep no dog away from a body left out all night. It is what prompts the Chorus's suggestion at l. 278. Notice that Sophocles gives the evidence for the miracle to the least imaginative witness available.

s3.quote: Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it,
s3.note: φύλαξ ἐλέγχων φύλακα (_phylax elenchōn phylaka_, 'guard accusing guard', l. 260): a small civil war among comrades, the morning after two brothers killed each other. The verb for their noise, ἐρρόθουν (_errothoun_, l. 259), 'they surged, muttered', returns in Creon's mouth at l. 290 for citizens he says are murmuring against him. Suspicion of everyone by everyone is what his Thebes sounds like at every level.

s3.quote: The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron,
s3.note: Lumps of hot metal, walking through fire, and θεοὺς ὁρκωμοτεῖν, 'to swear by the gods' (l. 265). With no evidence available the soldiers turn at once to the gods as judges, and it does not occur to them that the gods might be parties. Creon will swear by Zeus on the other side of the same question forty lines later.

s3.quote: And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds,
s3.note: The reeds are Storr's. The Greek has one man speak and all the rest bend their heads to the ground φόβῳ (_phobōi_, 'in fear', l. 270). Go back to l. 180, where Creon despised the man who locks his tongue 'from fear'. Here are his subjects an hour into his reign, afraid to tell him a fact. At l. 291 he complains that citizens shake their heads in secret, which is the same gesture seen from the throne.

s3.quote: And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize.
s3.note: πάλος (_palos_, 'the lot', l. 275) condemns him 'to win this good thing', τοῦτο τἀγαθὸν, with a soldier's sarcasm. The scapegoat is Storr's addition. The guards settle it by lot, the device Athens used to fill offices, and the lot produces a man who then argues with his king to his face. It is a small democratic procedure inside a play about one-man rule.

s3.quote: Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
s3.note: A jingle in the Greek, ἄκων οὐχ ἑκοῦσιν (_akōn ouch hekousin_, 'unwilling, to the unwilling', l. 276), and then another proverb. His verb is στέργει (_stergei_, 'loves', l. 277): nobody loves the bringer of bad words. Creon uses the same verb at l. 292 for what he wants from his subjects, necks under the yoke 'so as to love me'. The Guard knows he will not be loved; the king expects to be.

s3.quote: Of something more than natural at work.
s3.note: The word is θεήλατον (_theēlaton_, 'god-driven, sent by a god', l. 278), and Storr's phrase is too vague for it. The elders say this thought has been with them πάλαι, 'for some time', which means since the Guard began. It is their one unprompted religious instinct in the first half of the play and it is correct in spirit: the gods do turn out to want this burial. Creon silences it in a line, and it is Teiresias in [[s11]] who has to say it again before they will act on it.

s3.quote: O cease, you vex me with your babblement;
s3.note: Storr hides a tracked word. Creon says 'stop, before your talk fills me with ὀργῆς' (_orgēs_, 'anger', l. 280). _Orgē_ is temper, the passion that governs a man, and the ode will list ἀστυνόμους ὀργάς, 'the tempers that order cities', among human achievements (l. 356). Here is one such temper at work. He adds that they risk being found ἄνους τε καὶ γέρων, 'mindless as well as old'. Here the objection is age; with Haemon in [[s7]] it will be youth. No age turns out to be the right one for contradicting him.

s3.quote: That gods would have a thought for this dead man?
s3.note: πρόνοιαν (_pronoian_, 'forethought, care', l. 283). Here Creon stops speaking for the city and starts speaking for heaven. He calls the suggestion οὐκ ἀνεκτὰ, 'not to be borne', which is a statement about himself and not about the gods. He is sure he knows whom they despise. Teiresias exists in this play to tell him he does not.

s3.quote: And as some benefactor bury him,
s3.note: Follow the argument, because it is an argument: the gods honour benefactors, Polyneices came to burn their temples, therefore they cannot have honoured him. The hidden premise is that burial is a reward, to be earned by services like a civic crown. Antigone's reply in [[s5]] is that burial is owed to the dead as such, and that Hades does not sort them by their record. Creon models the gods on a city council and then finds that they vote as he does.

s3.quote: And scout their ordinances? Or perchance
s3.note: νόμους (_nomous_, l. 287): Polyneices came 'to scatter their land and laws'. Creon concedes in passing that the gods have _nomoi_ of their own. It is on precisely that ground that Antigone will stand, with laws unwritten and unfailing. He assumes the gods' laws and his own must coincide, and the ode's last stanza makes the same assumption at l. 367.

s3.quote: Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke,
s3.note: ὑπὸ ζυγῷ (_hypo zygōi_, 'under the yoke', l. 291) and λόφον (_lophon_, 'the neck', l. 292): his picture of a citizen is a draught animal that should keep its neck where it is put. The ode repeats both words at l. 351, where man's triumph is the yoke about the horse's neck. Either the Chorus are echoing their king or Sophocles is, and the echo makes the taming stanza sound like politics. Ask too how he can have 'long' noted this, πάλαι, on his first day. Perhaps he means the war, when he held command; perhaps suspicion supplies its own history.

s3.quote: By bribes. Of evils current upon earth
s3.note: Storr's 'current' is a hit. The Greek calls silver the worst _nomisma_ ever to grow among men (ll. 295–296), a word that means both 'coinage' and 'established custom' and shares its root with _nomos_. The noun for silver is ἄργυρος (_argyros_). The tirade that follows is stock moralising and good of its kind. Its fault is that it has no connection with the facts. Nobody has been paid, and he has a theory of the crime before he has a suspect.

s3.quote: Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home;
s3.note: Money πορθεῖ (_porthei_, 'sacks', l. 297) cities. An hour ago it was Polyneices who came to sack this one, for a throne. The enemy has changed from the invader to the coin without Creon remarking on it. For him every opponent turns out to be the same opponent, greed, and the list will grow to include his guards, his niece's accomplices, and a blind prophet.

s3.quote: And breeds a habit of dishonesty.
s3.note: Storr loses the religious word. Money teaches men to know δυσσέβειαν (_dyssebeian_, 'impiety', l. 301) in every act. Creon is the first to use it, and he uses it of men he imagines taking bribes to bury a corpse. Antigone speaks it last, on her way to the tomb in [[s9]]: by being pious she has earned the name of impiety. Between those two uses the play decides who was entitled to the word.

s3.quote: Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus,
s3.note: σέβας (_sebas_, 'reverence', l. 304), and he declares himself ὅρκιος, on oath. Literally: 'if Zeus still has reverence from me'. It is a strong form of oath, and the conditional is ugly in hindsight. He swears by Zeus to torture innocent men over a burial that Zeus's own laws, on Antigone's account, require.

s3.quote: Who carried out this lawless burial,
s3.note: 'Lawless' is Storr's; no such word is in the line. What is there is τὸν αὐτόχειρα τοῦδε τοῦ τάφου (_ton autocheira_, 'the one whose own hand did this burial', l. 306). _Autocheir_ is ordinarily the word for one who kills with his own hand, and Creon used it at l. 172 for the brothers' mutual slaughter. He reaches for the vocabulary of murder to describe covering a body. Antigone will accept the description; her whole claim is that her own hand did it.

s3.quote: Death for your punishment shall not suffice.
s3.note: 'Hades alone will not be enough for you' (l. 308). He treats Hades as an instrument within his gift, to be supplemented by torture when it is too mild. The ode answers within sixty lines: Hades is the single thing from which man contrives no escape (l. 360). He will use the same instrument on Antigone and find that it reaches his son and his wife.

s3.quote: Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make
s3.note: No cross in the Greek: ζῶντες κρεμαστοὶ (_zōntes kremastoi_, 'strung up alive', l. 309), until they reveal τήνδε ... ὕβριν (_hybrin_), 'this outrage'. It is the first _hybris_ in the play and it is Creon's name for a burial. He will use it twice of Antigone in [[s5]]. Mark what the test of l. 177 has produced within a hundred and fifty lines: a threat of torture against men he has no evidence against.

s3.quote: There are some villainies that bring no gain.
s3.note: τὸ κέρδος (l. 310) and τὸ κερδαίνειν (_to kerdainein_, 'profit-making', l. 312) inside three lines, with sarcasm: you will be tortured 'so that you may know where profit is to be got'. Add the hirelings and wages of ll. 294 and 302, the silver of l. 295 and l. 322, and κέρδη again at l. 326. That makes eight words for money in forty lines, about a deed done for nothing by someone who expects to die for it.

s3.quote: The many come to ruin and disgrace.
s3.note: ἀτωμένους (_atōmenous_, 'brought to ruin', l. 314) set against σεσωσμένους, 'saved': the same pair, _atē_ and safety, with which he defined his duty at ll. 185–186. He closes on a general maxim, as he usually does. It is true, and it is about him.

s3.quote: Is it thy ears that suffer, or thy heart?
s3.note: δάκνει (_daknei_, 'it bites', l. 317): 'in the ears, or in the soul, does it bite?' Something has changed in the Guard. Having heard an accusation he knows to be false, he is less afraid, and begins to examine the king like a doctor locating a pain. His answer two lines later is accurate and impertinent: the doer hurts your mind, I only hurt your ears. Creon's reply shows he cannot bear to be described.

s3.quote: What an inveterate babbler! get thee gone!
s3.note: λάλημα (_lalēma_, 'a piece of chatter', l. 320), a neuter noun, as if the man were a thing that makes noise. Watch Creon's habit: he does not answer what is said, he classifies the speaker. The elders are senile, the Guard is a chatterbox and a hireling, Ismene will be a viper, Haemon a woman's slave, Teiresias a profiteer. Each label saves him from weighing an argument.

s3.quote: Twice guilty, having sold thy soul for gain.
s3.note: τὴν ψυχὴν προδούς (_tēn psychēn prodous_, 'having betrayed your soul', l. 322), for silver. At l. 176 Creon said it is impossible to learn any man's ψυχήν, his soul, until he has been tested in office. He now reads a stranger's soul in four minutes and finds a bribe in it. The Guard's next line is the comment that this deserves.

s3.quote: Alas! how sad when reasoners reason wrong.
s3.note: ἦ δεινὸν (_ē deinon_, l. 323a): 'terrible indeed, when the one who judges judges falsely.' Storr's 'sad' is far too mild, and the word is the ode's word, spoken ten lines before the ode. The verb δοκεῖν (_dokein_) means to think or seem, and it is also the verb of resolutions, of what 'seems good' to a ruling body. So the line concerns a man whose opinions are decrees. The lowest person on stage tells the king the truth and the king hears only insolence. He is the first of several he outranks to do so.

s3.quote: The wages of ill-gotten gains is death.
s3.note: Storr has slipped St Paul into Sophocles. The Greek says only that τὰ δειλὰ κέρδη (_ta deila kerdē_, 'base gains', l. 326) 'produce pains', and death is not mentioned. It is a good example of how a 1912 verse translation gives a pagan king a Christian cadence. Creon leaves into the palace on this line, the fourth time in the scene he has ended a speech on profit.

s3.quote: Shalt see me here returning; that is sure.
s3.note: He is back within fifty lines, leading Antigone, and he opens [[s5]] by admitting that a man should swear to nothing. The joke has a point. In this play confident statements about the future are refuted quickly, the Guard's in fifty lines and Creon's by nightfall.

s3.quote: And for my safety owe the gods much thanks.
s3.note: σωθεὶς (_sōtheis_, 'saved', l. 331) and τοῖς θεοῖς: the scene began with the gods saving the city and ends with a soldier thanking them for saving his skin, ἐκτὸς ἐλπίδος, 'beyond hope'. His religion is simple and, as far as it goes, sound. Chance, he says at l. 328, will decide whether the man is caught: τύχη, where Creon sees a paid plot and the Chorus a god. With both actors gone the elders are alone, and what they have just heard, a deed with no visible doer, is what they sing about.

s4.quote: Many wonders there be,
s4.note: πολλὰ τὰ δεινὰ (_polla ta deina_, l. 333). _Deinos_ comes from the word for fear: terrible first, then awe-inspiring, then formidably clever, and never simply admirable. 'Wonders' keeps the sunny half. The Guard has used the word twice in the last hundred lines, both times for something frightening (ll. 243, 323a), so the audience hear the dark sense first. Aeschylus began an ode in the _Libation Bearers_ in almost the same way, about the many dread things earth breeds, and went on to human daring and passion as the worst of them. Sophocles' hearers knew that song.

s4.quote: but naught more wondrous than man;
s4.note: δεινότερον (_deinoteron_, l. 333) is a comparative: man does not stand outside the class of dreadful things, he tops it. The noun is ἀνθρώπου, the human being, not yet the male. Why do the elders sing this now? They have just heard of a deed done against a king's order by someone who left no trace. The ode is their response to that daring, which is the crux: is it a hymn to human progress, or a warning that the cleverest creature is the most dangerous? I think the first line already makes it the second, with the hymn carried inside it.

s4.quote: Over the surging sea, with a whitening south wind wan,
s4.note: The first art is seafaring, and it is reckless from the start: the sea is πολιοῦ (_poliou_, 'grey', l. 334) and the wind is χειμερίῳ νότῳ, the stormy south wind of winter, when sensible Greeks kept their ships ashore. Man is called τοῦτο, 'this thing', a neuter, as though the Chorus were pointing at a specimen. The ship comes first in the list, and we have just listened to a ruler who thinks of his city as one.

s4.quote: Through the foam of the firth, man makes his perilous way;
s4.note: περῶν (_perōn_, 'passing through', l. 336) picks up πέραν (_peran_, 'across', l. 334): man is the creature that crosses. Storr's 'perilous' is his own, though fair, since the swells are περιβρυχίοισιν, 'engulfing'. Keep the idea of passage in mind. The second strophe turns it into a single word, 'all-passing', and then names the one crossing from which nobody finds a way back.

s4.quote: And the eldest of deities Earth that knows not toil nor decay
s4.note: The Greek is θεῶν τε τὰν ὑπερτάταν, Γᾶν (l. 337), 'the highest of the gods, Earth', which is a claim of rank where Storr has one of age. She is ἄφθιτον, ἀκαμάταν, imperishable and unwearied. Even so she is man's object. And it is earth, a handful of it, that has just been scattered on Polyneices; the ode and the crime share a substance. One act does violence to her and the other gives the dead back to her.

s4.quote: Ever he furrows and scores, as his team, year in year out,
s4.note: ἀποτρύεται (_apotryetai_, 'he wears away', l. 338). The verb is harsh and it is set right against 'unwearied': he wears out the one who cannot be worn. A song of plain praise would not describe ploughing as attrition of the highest goddess. ἔτος εἰς ἔτος, 'year into year', makes it relentless.

s4.quote: With breed of the yoked horse, the ploughshare turneth about.
s4.note: ἱππείῳ γένει (_hippeiōi genei_, 'with the offspring of horses', l. 340) is usually taken to mean mules, the standard plough-animal, which are themselves a human contrivance. The yoke in Storr's line is imported from the next stanza, where it belongs. Note the pattern so far: sea and earth are both elements that are also gods, and both are treated as material.

s4.quote: The light-witted birds of the air, the beasts of the weald and the wood
s4.note: κουφονόων (_kouphonoōn_, 'light-minded', l. 343): the birds lose because they think lightly, and man wins by thought. The verb for what he does to them is ἄγει (_agei_, 'leads off', l. 343), the word for carrying away captives. When Antigone is brought in at the end of this section the guards ἄγουσι, 'are leading', her (l. 382), and in [[s5]] the Guard says they 'hunted' her and compares her cry to a bird's over an emptied nest. The elders sing of snaring creatures while the snare is closing on someone they know.

s4.quote: He traps with his woven snare, and the brood of the briny flood.
s4.note: σπείραισι δικτυοκλώστοις (_speiraisi diktyoklōstois_, 'coils of woven net', l. 346), a showpiece compound, the language itself knotted like the mesh. Air, land and sea each give up their creatures, so the conquest is total across the three realms. Hunting is the first human activity in the ode that is directed at other living things, and it is done by enclosure.

s4.quote: Master of cunning he: the savage bull, and the hart
s4.note: περιφραδὴς ἀνήρ (_periphradēs anēr_, 'man, thoughtful all round', l. 347). The noun has changed: the ode began with the human being and now says ἀνήρ, the male. The elders, like Creon, picture the burier as a man. Then κρατεῖ δὲ μηχαναῖς (_kratei de mēchanais_, l. 348), 'he masters by devices', and _kratos_ is the word Creon used twice for his own power at ll. 166 and 173. Storr's hart is not in the Greek, which has only 'the beast that roams the hills'.

s4.quote: And the shaggy rough-maned steed is broken to bear the bit.
s4.note: The Greek has no bit: the horse is tamed with ζυγῶν (_zygōn_, 'yoking') ἀμφὶ λόφον, 'about its neck' (l. 351), and the bull is ἀκμῆτα (_akmēta_, 'untired', l. 352), like the unwearied earth before it. Yoke and neck are the two words Creon used for his subjects at ll. 291–292. Storr's bit arrives all the same in [[s5]], where Creon says of Antigone that spirited horses are schooled with a small one. The stanza on taming animals is, word for word, the king's theory of government.

s4.quote: Speech and the wind-swift speed of counsel
s4.note: φθέγμα (_phthegma_, 'voice, speech', l. 354) and ἀνεμόεν φρόνημα (_anemoen phronēma_, 'thought like the wind'). There is _phronēma_ again, Creon's word for his own cast of mind at l. 207. Wind-swift is praise, but wind is also what changes direction and blows ships off course, and Creon's thinking in the last scene moved very fast indeed. Speech stands first among the inward arts, in a play where nearly every scene is a contest of speeches and no one is persuaded until too late.

s4.quote: and civic wit,
s4.note: Storr has tamed this. The Greek is ἀστυνόμους ὀργάς (_astynomous orgas_, ll. 354–356), 'the tempers that give law to towns'. _Orgē_ is disposition, passion, and commonly anger: it is the word Creon used at l. 280 when the Chorus's piety began to fill him with it. And _nomos_ sits inside the adjective. So the Chorus count among man's wonders the very thing we have just watched, a city-ruling temper, and the phrase can be heard with a shudder.

s4.quote: He hath learnt for himself all these; and the arrowy rain to fly
s4.note: ἐδιδάξατο (_edidaxato_, 'he taught himself', l. 356). No god gives any of this. In the _Prometheus Bound_ every art is the gift of Prometheus; here man is his own teacher, which is the account of progress associated with thinkers such as Protagoras. The absence of the gods as givers is the most striking thing about the list, and the last stanza supplies them only as a limit. The play's closing lines return to teaching: great blows teach good sense in old age.

s4.quote: And the nipping airs that freeze, ’neath the open winter sky.
s4.note: Housing, the last of the outward arts, is put negatively: he has learned φεύγειν (_pheugein_, 'to flee', l. 357) the shafts of frost and rain. It is the first of three words for flight within five lines, with φεῦξιν at l. 360 and φυγὰς at l. 361. Under the mastery, human skill turns out to be a set of escapes. The sentence is being built so that the one thing without an escape arrives with full weight.

s4.quote: He hath provision for all:
s4.note: παντοπόρος· ἄπορος (_pantoporos; aporos_, l. 358): 'all-resourceful; resourceless', set side by side with only a pause between. The usual construal joins the second to what follows: 'without resource he meets nothing that is to come'. But the ear takes the two words together first, and the jolt is meant. The same device closes the ode with ὑψίπολις· ἄπολις. _Poros_ is a way through, so the crosser of seas from the first stanza has become the one who finds a passage everywhere.

s4.quote: fell plague he hath learnt to endure;
s4.note: Storr has reversed the order and weakened the verb. In the Greek death comes first and medicine after, as a concession: 'yet from baffling diseases he has contrived escapes', ξυμπέφρασται (l. 361). He does not endure them, he thinks his way out. The diseases are ἀμηχάνων (_amēchanōn_, 'without remedy'), the word Creon used at l. 175 for the impossibility of knowing a man's soul. Even what has no device, man has found a device for, with the one exception.

s4.quote: yet for death he hath found no cure.
s4.note: Ἅιδα μόνον φεῦξιν οὐκ ἐπάξεται (_Haida monon pheuxin ouk epaxetai_, l. 360): 'from Hades alone he will procure no escape.' This is the hinge of the ode, and the one thing man has not mastered is named as a god, Hades, where Storr has 'death'. The verb is future: he never will. Creon said at l. 308 that 'Hades alone' would not suffice as a punishment and is about to use death as an instrument of policy twice. He learns that it does not stay where it is put. The dead man lying on the plain belongs to the one power the arts cannot reach, and that is what the edict ignores.

s4.quote: Passing the wildest flight thought are the cunning and skill,
s4.note: Here is the summary of the list: σοφόν τι τὸ μηχανόεν τέχνας (_sophon ti to mēchanoen technas_, l. 365), 'a clever thing, the inventiveness of art', possessed _hyper elpida_, beyond expectation. Count the _technai_: sailing, ploughing, fowling, hunting, fishing, taming, speech, thought, civic order, building, medicine. Now ask what is missing. Reverence and justice are not among them. In the myth Plato gives Protagoras, those have to be sent separately by Zeus because the arts alone leave men destroying one another. The last stanza is about that gap.

s4.quote: That guide man now to the light, but now to counsels of ill.
s4.note: Storr puts the good first; the Greek puts the bad: τοτὲ μὲν κακόν, 'now to evil', then to good (l. 366). And the verb is ἕρπει (_herpei_, 'he creeps, he moves along'), a slow word after so much crossing and outrunning. Skill has no direction of its own. This sentence is the plainest evidence that the ode is not a hymn, since four stanzas of achievement end in a coin-toss.

s4.quote: If he honors the laws of the land,
s4.note: νόμους ... χθονὸς (_nomous chthonos_, l. 367). The participle in this text, γεραίρων (_gerairōn_, 'honouring'), is an editor's correction; the manuscripts have a word meaning 'weaving in', which some keep. χθονός is 'of the land', and that is what the elders mean: the law of Thebes, which today is Creon's edict. But _chthōn_ is also the earth and what lies beneath it, and the gods below are the chthonic ones. The phrase can mean the laws Antigone obeys, though the singers do not know it.

s4.quote: and reveres the Gods of the State
s4.note: A mistranslation that takes Creon's side. The Greek is θεῶν τʼ ἔνορκον δίκαν, 'and the justice of the gods, sworn by oath' (l. 367). The word is δίκαν (_dikan_, 'justice'), and there is no State in it. The Chorus name two things, the laws of the land and the gods' justice, and assume they are one, so that honouring both is a single act. The whole play happens in the space between them. In [[s5]] Antigone will appeal to the Justice who dwells with the gods below, against the law of the land.

s4.quote: Proudly his city shall stand;
s4.note: ὑψίπολις (_hypsipolis_, l. 370), one word, and ambiguous: 'high in his city' or 'having a high city'. Storr chooses the second. I prefer the first, because the next word is about a person. Creon believes this stanza describes him, since by his _nomoi_ he makes the city great (l. 191). The Chorus probably believe it too, at this point.

s4.quote: but a cityless outcast I rate
s4.note: ἄπολις (_apolis_, l. 370), set directly against ὑψίπολις with only a stop between, like 'all-resourceful; resourceless' above. Whom does it condemn? In the singers' minds, the unknown burier who defied the edict. In the event it fits two people. Antigone becomes literally cityless, at home among neither the living nor the dead, as she says in [[s9]]. Creon, who dishonoured the gods' justice while enforcing the law of the land, ends [[s13]] asking to be led away, a man who is nothing. The elders think they are describing a criminal and have described the alternatives open to their king.

s4.quote: Whoso bold in his pride from the path of right doth depart;
s4.note: Two phrases matter. τὸ μὴ καλὸν (_to mē kalon_, 'what is not fine', l. 370): in [[s1]] Antigone used exactly that adjective for dying in this act. And τόλμας χάριν (_tolmas charin_, 'for daring's sake', l. 371), which answers Creon's 'who dared?' at l. 248. So the vocabulary points at the burier. The question the play puts is which of the two, the girl with the dust or the king with the edict, was keeping company with what is not _kalon_.

s4.quote: Ne’er may I sit by his side, or share the thoughts of his heart.
s4.note: παρέστιος (_parestios_, 'at my hearth', l. 371) and ἴσον φρονῶν (_ison phronōn_, 'thinking the same', l. 375), with _phronein_ once more. This is a formula of excommunication: the offender is to be kept from the household fire as one keeps away a polluted man. The irony needs no forcing. These elders will share Creon's counsels for another seven hundred lines, and the pollution, when it comes, comes from his act.

s4.quote: What strange vision meets my eyes,
s4.note: The metre changes to marching anapaests as the Guard leads Antigone in. Their words are δαιμόνιον τέρας (_daimonion teras_, 'a portent from the gods', l. 376), and ἀμφινοῶ, 'I am of two minds'. A _teras_ is a prodigy, one more _deinon_, and they have no idea how apt the adjective is. The staging is the comment on the ode: four stanzas on what 'man' dares, and the answer that walks in is a girl.

s4.quote: Hapless child of hapless sire,
s4.note: δυστήνου πατρὸς Οἰδιπόδα (l. 380): they identify her through her father before she has said a word in their presence, as they will again at l. 471 once she has spoken, and as [[s6|the next ode]] will at length. For the elders the explanation of Antigone is heredity. It is kinder than Creon's explanation, money, and it is equally a way of not listening to what she is about to say.

s4.quote: Madly brave the King’s decree?
s4.note: Three words in the Greek settle the Chorus's position for now. She is ἀπιστοῦσαν (_apistousan_, 'disobeying', l. 381), Creon's participle from l. 219. What she disobeys is τοῖς βασιλείοισιν ... νόμοις (l. 382), 'the royal laws', so the proclamation has become _nomoi_, fifteen lines after 'the laws of the land'. And she was taken ἐν ἀφροσύνῃ (_en aphrosynēi_, 'in folly', l. 383), the absence of _phronein_. They have judged before the hearing. Yet they call her 'child' twice and sound appalled, and that divided response is the one they keep until the end.
